cvrr: from CVR numbers to accounting data

Source: R/cvrr-package.R
cvrr-package.Rd

Danish annual reports are public documents, and Erhvervsstyrelsen publishes them through a free distribution service. cvrr is the route from a list of CVR numbers to data you can analyse: build a query, send it, flatten the response, download the documents, and parse the machine-readable ones.

The pipeline

Six calls from a list of CVR numbers to the tables an analysis reads. Each takes what the previous one returned.

library(cvrr)

cvr_query(
  cvr          = c("12345678", "87654321"),
  enddate_from = "2020-01-01",
  enddate_to   = "2024-12-31"
) |>
  cvr_search(contact = "you@example.com") |>
  cvr_hits() |>
  cvr_download("materiale/xbrl")

# a whole directory, taxonomy and all
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")

a <- xbrl_accounts(x)
a$company           # who the company is
a$location          # where it is
a$audit             # who audited it, who filed it, with what tool
a$checks            # whether any of it adds up
a$income_statement  # lines, in statement order
a$balance           # lines, with the ones the filer left out derived
a$movements         # the fixed asset note, movement by movement
a$prose             # what management wrote

Every table opens with the same key – cvr, name, period_start, period_end – so moving between them needs no looking.

Everything else in the package is either a step of that route taken on its own, or a way of asking whether a filing's figures add up.

Two forms, one useful

A filing usually exists as both a PDF and an XML file. The XML is XBRL, the machine-readable form, and read_xbrl() turns it into a tibble with one row per reported fact, its context and its unit. That is the whole route: no manual step.

The PDF is the human-readable version, and there is no parser for it here. For older filings, small companies, and scanned reports it is the only digital trace, and turning one back into a table is a different kind of work – taxmill is about that.

What the filing does not say

An instance carries facts, contexts and units – and no readable text. Every label, the statement hierarchy, and the debit/credit marking of each element live in the taxonomy the filing names in a single schemaRef. That URI is an identifier, not a download address, so the package is obtained separately and resolved locally: read_taxonomy() opens it, add_taxonomy() joins a filing to it, and check_statement() reconciles the result.

It also settles a question the instance answers only by omission. Group figures are tagged; parent-company figures are not tagged at all, and reading their absence correctly depends on the dimension default the taxonomy declares.

Signs

XBRL amounts often arrive without a meaningful sign: costs can be reported as positive numbers, and the convention varies between preparers. find_signs() recovers them, because an income statement has to reconcile – it searches for the +1/-1/0 assignment that makes the line items sum to the reported total. It knows nothing about XBRL and works on any labelled values with a total.

Using the service well

cvr_search() requires a contact email address and sends it as the User-Agent header, because Erhvervsstyrelsen asks requests to identify their sender. The function refuses an empty contact, but it cannot check that the address is honest – that part is yours. vignette("cvrr") covers the rest of the habits worth having: query volume, scroll for complete results, testing small first, and the legal frame.

The functions

  • Find and fetch: cvr_query(), cvr_search(), cvr_hits(), cvr_download()

  • Read: read_xbrl() – one filing, a list of them, or a directory, with the taxonomy resolved on the way in

  • Divide up: xbrl_accounts(), and xbrl_company(), xbrl_lines() and xbrl_movements() for one table at a time

  • Name and place: add_taxonomy(), read_taxonomy(), cvrr_taxonomy_tables

  • Derive: xbrl_fill() and xbrl_resolve(), which xbrl_lines() uses and which can be run on their own

  • Reconcile: check_statement(), check_breakdown(), check_cascade(), check_movement(), check_continuity(), check_inclusion(), find_signs()

  • Read the notes: xbrl_note_tables(), xbrl_period()

The package stops at the accounting figures. Mapping them onto a statistic's own variable definitions is the user's to make, and depends on the definitions in force.
